So last class we discussed the transformation of religious worldview during the course of western history. At first there was the mother goddess, then transitioned to polytheism, and eventually monotheism.

During this transition, our minds perceived the world differently in three key aspects. First, before we understood that mind led to matter; the universe is just one giant mind that vibrates, with atoms created by the intersection of these vibrations. However, today in science class, you're taught that the brain creates the mind. This conception is very problematic and will be discussed throughout the semester.

The second major difference was our understanding of the world being metaphorical. We saw forces we couldn't see or feel but believed were there, naming them gods. Now everything must be literal; if you can’t measure it, it doesn't exist. The third big change is that before we trusted intuition and our senses, but today in science class, you're taught to trust data, tools, and theory over your own eyes.

This is why school is so hard—humans are designed to learn and absorb information, but the ideas taught often go against our natural intuition. These were the main concepts from last class, now let's move on to mind control.

We'll start by going back to the four earliest civilizations: China, Indus Valley civilization (Harappan), Mesopotamia, and Egypt. Of these, Egypt was for thousands of years the most powerful, wealthiest, and influential. In a mass society, social control is critical. Each society had different solutions.

In China, they developed a bureaucracy based on the kju, or civil service examination, ensuring everyone's focus was on getting their child to pass to become an official, which provided social stability. This system still exists today under the name gao.

The IVC created religion that preached egalitarianism and peacefulness, becoming the prototype for Buddhism. Mesopotamia’s solution was war, as there were no natural defenses; centuries of warfare kept society together. In Egypt, the Pharaoh was believed to be a god, enforcing obedience. However, the pharaoh was human, so his life was always at risk.

Now, what does it take to be a great leader?
